title: Foolish Wives

evidence.note: Published January 11, 1922 by Universal. Under the 95-year US term, works published in 1923 were the first to enter the public domain in 2019 (per Duke CSPD), so a 1922 publication has already expired and the print is public domain in the US.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2019

evidence.note: The film is silent. Sigmund Romberg's original score is credited, but modern copies usually carry a newer recorded score. The 2020 San Francisco Silent Film Festival/MoMA restoration uses a Timothy Brock score performed by the Real Filharmonía de Galicia (DCP version), which is a separate recording and may be protected.
Original screenplay by Erich von Stroheim, not an adaptation, so there is no separate source work whose term could outlast the film's.

The San Francisco Silent Film Festival/MoMA restoration used a tinted nitrate print with Italian intertitles from Cineteca Italiana, a 1928 re-edited MoMA print, and a script and piano score from the Library of Congress. It adds newly created intertitles in Universal Super-Jewel style and a new Timothy Brock orchestral score. A faithful image restoration adds no new US copyright, but the new titles and score may be protected.

watch.label: Erich Von Stroheim's Foolish Wives (1922), about 130-minute version

editorial:
Foolish Wives is a 1922 American silent drama written and directed by Erich von Stroheim for Universal, with von Stroheim also playing the con-artist Count Karamzin on a Hollywood-built Monte Carlo. It was released on January 11, 1922. Von Stroheim's original cut ran about six hours. Universal's release ran about 117 minutes, and what survives is a reconstruction from several prints. A creator would want it for the sets, the notoriety and the Romberg-era Universal pedigree. The screenplay was original, so no earlier book or play adds a second copyright.

The print is public domain in the US because of its 1922 publication. The trap is the version you copy. The 2020 San Francisco Silent Film Festival/MoMA restoration carries a new Timothy Brock score and newly created intertitles, and those additions may be protected even though the underlying images are not. Use a scan of a plain archival copy, such as the Internet Archive items, or clear the music and titles separately. No trademark has been researched for this title.
faq: Can I reuse a Foolish Wives clip in my own video?

The 1922 images are public domain in the US. Check the copy you take it from. A restored release can add a new score and new intertitles that are not free to reuse, so pair a clean copy with your own music.
Is the modern restoration free to copy?

Not as a whole. A faithful restoration of the picture adds no new US copyright, but the new Timothy Brock score and the new intertitles in the San Francisco Silent Film Festival/MoMA restoration may be protected. Do not rip a copy-protected disc, because that can break the DMCA.
